en: The Sūtra on the Differentiation of Karmic Retribution Spoken by the Buddha for the Elder Śuka, translated during the Sui dynasty by Gao-tan Fa-zhi, Governor of Yangchuan Commandery.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the elder Śuka, son of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, saying: "Elder Śuka!
I shall explain for you the Dharma-gate of the distinctions between the retributions of wholesome and unwholesome karma."
"You should listen attentively and reflect upon it well!
At that time, Śuka addressed the Buddha, saying,
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
"I wish to hear it with joy!
The Buddha told Śuka:
"All sentient beings are bound by karma, dependent upon karma, and revolve according to their own karma."
Due to these causes and conditions, there are distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior.
"There may be karma that causes sentient beings to receive the retribution of a short life;
there may be karma that causes sentient beings to receive the retribution of a long life."
"There is karma that can cause sentient beings to receive the retribution of much illness;
there is karma that can cause sentient beings to receive the retribution of little illness.
There is karma that can cause sentient beings to receive the retribution of ugliness;"
There are some karmas that can cause sentient beings to obtain the retribution of physical beauty;
there are some karmas that can cause sentient beings to obtain the retribution of minor power and influence;
and there are some karmas that can cause sentient beings to obtain the retribution of great power and influence.
"There is karma that can cause sentient beings to obtain the retribution of birth into a low-born family;
there is karma that can cause sentient beings to obtain the retribution of birth into a high-born family.
There is karma that can cause sentient beings to obtain the retribution of meager means of subsistence;"
There may be karma that causes sentient beings to obtain the retribution of abundant material resources;
there may be karma that causes sentient beings to obtain the retribution of false wisdom;
and there may be karma that causes sentient beings to obtain the retribution of right wisdom.
“Some karma can cause sentient beings to receive retribution in the hells;
some karma can cause sentient beings to receive retribution as animals;
and some karma can cause sentient beings to receive retribution as hungry ghosts.”
There are some karmas that can cause sentient beings to receive the retribution of asuras;
there are some karmas that can cause sentient beings to receive the retribution of the human realm;
and there are some karmas that can cause sentient beings to receive the retribution of the desire-realm heavens.
There are some karmas that can cause sentient beings to obtain the retribution of the form heavens;
there are some karmas that can cause sentient beings to obtain the retribution of the formless heavens;
and there are some karmas that can cause sentient beings to obtain determinate retribution.
There may be karma that causes sentient beings to receive an indeterminate retribution;
there may be karma that causes sentient beings to receive retribution in a borderland;
and there may be karma that causes sentient beings to receive retribution in a central land.
"There are some karmas that cause sentient beings to exhaust the full lifespan of hell;
there are some karmas that cause sentient beings to experience half the lifespan of hell;
and there are some karmas that cause sentient beings to enter [hell] briefly and then emerge immediately."
"There may be karma that is performed but not accumulated;
there may be karma that is accumulated but not performed;
there may be karma that is both performed and accumulated."
There may be karma that is neither performed nor accumulated.
There may be karma that causes sentient beings to experience happiness first and suffering later;
there may be karma that causes sentient beings to experience suffering first and happiness later.
There are some karmas that cause sentient beings to suffer both at the beginning and at the end;
there are some karmas that cause sentient beings to experience happiness both at the beginning and at the end.
"There are some karmas that cause sentient beings to be poor yet joyful in giving;..."
There is karma that causes sentient beings to be wealthy yet stingy and greedy;
there is karma that causes sentient beings to be wealthy and able to practice generosity;
and there is karma that causes sentient beings to be poor and stingy and greedy.
“There may be karma that enables sentient beings to obtain physical pleasure while their minds are not pleased;
there may be karma that enables sentient beings to obtain mental pleasure while their bodies are not pleased;
and there may be karma that enables sentient beings to obtain both physical and mental pleasure.”
There may be karma that causes sentient beings to experience neither pleasure in body nor pleasure in mind.
There may be karma that causes sentient beings' lives to come to an end while their karma does not;
there may be karma that causes sentient beings' karma to come to an end while their lives do not.
There are some karmas that can cause both the karma and the life-span of sentient beings to be exhausted together;
there are also some karmas that can cause neither the karma nor the life-span of sentient beings to be exhausted, and which are able to sever all afflictions.
"There are some karmas that cause sentient beings to be born in the evil realms with exquisite forms, handsome eyes, and radiant skin, such that people delight in seeing them;
there are some karmas that cause sentient beings to be born in the evil realms with ugly forms, coarse and rough skin, such that people do not rejoice in seeing them;
and there are some karmas that cause sentient beings to be born in the evil realms with foul-smelling bodies and mouths, and with impaired sense faculties."
“Some sentient beings practice the ten unwholesome actions and receive external retributive results that are evil;
some sentient beings practice the ten kinds of wholesome actions and receive external retributive results that are superior.”
"Furthermore, householder!
If there are sentient beings who pay homage to the stupas and temples of the Buddha, they shall obtain ten kinds of merit;
if they offer precious canopies as gifts, they shall obtain ten kinds of merit."
By making offerings of silk banners, one obtains ten kinds of merit;
by making offerings of bells and chimes, one obtains ten kinds of merit;
by making offerings of robes, one obtains ten kinds of merit.
By making an offering of vessels, one obtains ten kinds of merit;
by making an offering of food and drink, one obtains ten kinds of merit;
by making an offering of boots and shoes, one obtains ten kinds of merit.
By offering incense and flowers, one attains ten kinds of merit;
by offering lamps and light, one attains ten kinds of merit;
by reverently joining the palms, one attains ten kinds of merit.
"This is called the brief exposition of the Dharma-gate on the distinctions among the various karmas of the world.
The Buddha told Śuka:
"There are ten kinds of karma that cause sentient beings to receive the retribution of a short lifespan:"
First, personally committing the act of killing;
second, exhorting others to kill;
third, praising the method of killing.
Fourth, seeing killing and rejoicing in it;
fifth, harboring malice toward those one hates and wishing for their destruction;
sixth, feeling joy in one's heart when an enemy has been destroyed.
Seventh, destroying the fetal development of others;
eighth, instructing others to destroy it;
ninth, establishing celestial temples and slaughtering sentient beings;
Tenth, teaching others to engage in battle and to harm one another.
By these ten karmas, one receives the retribution of a short lifespan.
Furthermore, there are ten karmas that can cause sentient beings to receive the retribution of a long lifespan:
First, one does not kill living beings oneself;
second, one encourages others not to kill;
third, one praises the abstention from killing.
Fourth, seeing others refrain from killing, one gives rise to joy in one's heart;
fifth, seeing those who are being killed, one employs skillful means to rescue and spare them;
sixth, seeing those terrified of death, one comforts their minds.
Seventh, seeing those who are terrified, one bestows fearlessness upon them;
eighth, seeing those afflicted by various ailments and sufferings, one gives rise to a heart of compassion and pity;
ninth, seeing those in urgent distress, one gives rise to a heart of great compassion.
Tenth, by bestowing various foods and drinks upon sentient beings.
Through these ten karmas, one obtains the retribution of a long life.
Furthermore, there are ten karmas that cause sentient beings to receive the retribution of much illness:
First, taking pleasure in beating and striking all sentient beings;
second, exhorting others to beat them;
third, praising the act of beating.
Fourth, they rejoice when seeing others being beaten;
fifth, they trouble and disturb their parents, causing them mental distress and anxiety;
sixth, they trouble and disturb the noble and holy ones.
Seventh, seeing an enemy suffer from illness, one feels great joy in one's heart;
eighth, seeing an enemy recover from illness, one feels displeasure in one's heart;
ninth, at the bedside of an enemy who is ill, one administers unwholesome medicine.
Tenth, when previous food has not yet been digested, one eats again.
By these ten karmas, one receives the retribution of many illnesses.
Furthermore, there are ten karmas that can cause sentient beings to receive the retribution of having few illnesses:
First, one does not take pleasure in beating or striking any sentient being;
second, one encourages others not to beat them;
third, one praises the practice of not beating.
Fourth, seeing those who do not strike others, one gives rise to joy in the heart;
fifth, making offerings to one's parents and to all who are ill;
sixth, seeing the illness of sages and holy ones, attending to and making offerings to them.
Seventh, seeing an enemy’s illness cured, one gives rise to a heart of joy;
eighth, seeing those suffering from illness, one bestows excellent medicine upon them and also encourages others to do so;
ninth, toward sentient beings who suffer from illness, one gives rise to a mind of compassion and pity.
Tenth, one is able to exercise self-restraint regarding all food and drink.
Through these ten karmas, one receives the retribution of having few illnesses.
Furthermore, there are ten karmas that cause sentient beings to receive the retribution of ugliness:
First, they take pleasure in practicing anger;
second, they take pleasure in harboring resentment;
third, they deceive and delude others.
Fourth, they disturb and vex sentient beings;
fifth, they lack love and reverence toward their parents;
sixth, they do not give rise to respect for the worthy and the noble.
Seventh, they plunder the livelihoods, fields, and properties of the worthy and holy;
eighth, they extinguish the lamps at the stupas and temples of the Buddha;
ninth, upon seeing those who are ugly or deformed, they revile and despise them.
Tenth, practicing various evil deeds.
By means of these ten karmas, one receives the retribution of ugliness.
Furthermore, there are ten karmas that can cause sentient beings to receive the retribution of physical beauty:
First, being free from anger;
second, giving clothing;
third, loving and respecting one's parents.
Fourth, to honor and respect the worthy and holy ones;
fifth, to anoint and adorn the stupas;
sixth, to sweep and sprinkle the halls and chambers.
Seventh, to sweep and sprinkle the grounds of the Saṃgha;
eighth, to sweep and sprinkle the stupas of the Buddha;
ninth, upon seeing those who are unattractive, not to give rise to contempt or disdain, but to arouse a heart of reverence.
Tenth, seeing those who are handsome leads to awakening to past causes.
Through these ten karmas, one obtains the retribution of physical beauty.
Furthermore, there are ten karmas that can cause sentient beings to obtain the retribution of minor power:
First, giving rise to a mind of envy toward all sentient beings;
second, feeling mental distress and feverish agitation upon seeing others obtain benefit;
third, feeling joy in one's heart upon seeing others suffer loss.
Fourth, to give rise to a mind of jealousy and malice toward the reputation of others;
fifth, to feel great joy upon seeing others lose their reputation;
sixth, to retreat from the bodhicitta and to deface images of the Buddha.
Seventh, having no intention to serve one's own parents or the noble and holy ones;
eighth, encouraging others to cultivate deeds of little majesty and virtue;
ninth, obstructing others from practicing deeds of great majesty and virtue.
Tenth, seeing those with little majesty and virtue, one gives rise to a mind of contempt and disdain.
By these ten karmas, one receives the retribution of having little majesty and power.
Furthermore, there are ten karmas that can cause sentient beings to obtain the retribution of great majesty and power:
First, to have no envy in one's heart toward any sentient beings;
second, to feel joy in one's heart upon seeing others obtain benefit;
third, to give rise to a mind of compassion upon seeing others suffer loss.
Fourth, one feels joy in the reputation of others;
fifth, seeing others lose their reputation, one assists them in harboring sorrow and distress;
sixth, one generates the bodhicitta, creates images of the Buddha, and offers precious parasols as gifts.
Seventh, to respectfully welcome and receive one’s own parents as well as the worthy and holy ones;
eighth, to exhort others to abandon deeds of little majesty and virtue;
ninth, to exhort others to practice deeds of great majesty and virtue.
Tenth, seeing those who lack majesty and power, one does not treat them with contempt.
By these ten karmic actions, one obtains the retribution of great majesty and power.
Furthermore, there are ten karmic actions that cause sentient beings to obtain birth in a lowly family:
First, not knowing how to respect one's father;
second, not knowing how to respect one's mother;
third, not knowing how to respect śramaṇas.
Fourth, not knowing how to revere brahmins;
fifth, failing to show respect and veneration toward one's elders;
sixth, failing to welcome and make offerings to one's teachers and preceptors.
Seventh, seeing elders and superiors, one does not rise to greet them nor invite them to be seated;
eighth, toward one's parents, one does not comply with their instructions;
ninth, even toward the worthy and the noble, one does not accept their teachings.
Tenth, to despise those of low birth.
By these ten karmic actions, one receives the retribution of being born into a low-born family.
Furthermore, there are ten karmic actions that can cause sentient beings to receive the retribution of being born into a high-born family:
First, knowing well how to revere one's father;
second, knowing well how to revere one's mother;
third, knowing well how to revere śramaṇas.
Fourth, skillfully knowing how to revere brahmins;
fifth, reverently protecting one's elders;
sixth, respectfully welcoming one's teachers and superiors.
Seventh, upon seeing elders and superiors, one should rise to greet them and invite them to be seated;
eighth, in the presence of one's parents, one should respectfully receive their instructions;
ninth, in the presence of the worthy and holy, one should honor them and receive their teachings.
Tenth, not disparaging those of low birth.
Through these ten karmas, one receives the retribution of being born into a noble family.
Furthermore, there are ten karmas that cause sentient beings to receive the retribution of having few resources for livelihood:
First, committing theft oneself;
second, encouraging others to commit theft; third, praising theft.
Fourth, they take delight in the theft of views;
fifth, they diminish the livelihood and resources of their parents;
sixth, they plunder the wealth and provisions of the noble and holy ones.
Seventh, seeing others obtain benefit, one’s mind does not rejoice;
eighth, obstructing others from obtaining benefit by creating hindrances for them;
ninth, seeing others practice giving, one lacks a heart of sympathetic joy.
Tenth, seeing famine in the world, one feels no compassion but instead gives rise to joy.
Through these ten karmas, one obtains the retribution of having meager means of subsistence.
Furthermore, there are ten karmas that can cause sentient beings to obtain the retribution of abundant means of subsistence:
First, one refrains from stealing oneself;
second, one encourages others not to steal;
third, one praises the abstention from stealing.
Fourth, seeing others refrain from stealing, one gives rise to joy in one’s heart;
fifth, providing for one’s parents’ livelihood;
sixth, bestowing upon the worthy and holy whatever they require.
Seventh, seeing others obtain benefit, one gives rise to joy in the heart;
eighth, seeing those who seek benefit, one provides assistance through skillful means;
ninth, seeing those who delight in giving, one gives rise to gladness in the heart.
Tenth, seeing the world suffering from famine, one gives rise to a heart of compassion.
By these ten karmas, one obtains the retribution of abundant means of subsistence.
Furthermore, there are ten karmas that can cause sentient beings to obtain the retribution of false wisdom:
First, they are unable to consult with wise śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas;
second, they openly proclaim unwholesome dharmas;
third, they are unable to receive, uphold, and practice the true Dharma.
Fourth, praising what are not fixed dharmas as being fixed dharmas;
fifth, begrudging the Dharma and refusing to teach it;
sixth, associating with those of false wisdom.
Seventh, they distance themselves from right knowledge;
eighth, they praise wrong views;
ninth, they abandon right view.
Tenth, seeing foolish and evil people, one treats them with contempt and slanders them.
Through these ten karmas, one receives the retribution of false wisdom.
Furthermore, there are ten karmas that can cause sentient beings to receive the retribution of right wisdom:
First, being well able to consult with wise śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas;
second, clearly expounding the wholesome dharmas;
third, hearing and retaining the true dharma.
Fourth, upon seeing one who speaks of the definitive Dharma, they exclaim, "Excellent!
Fifth, they delight in expounding the true Dharma;
sixth, they draw near to those of right wisdom.
Seventh, to uphold and protect the true Dharma;
eighth, to diligently cultivate extensive learning;
ninth, to remain far removed from false views.
Tenth, upon seeing a foolish and evil person, one does not give rise to contempt or disdain.
Through these ten karmas, one obtains the retribution of right knowledge.
Furthermore, there are ten karmas that cause sentient beings to receive the retribution of hell:
First, committing grave evil deeds with the body;
second, committing grave evil deeds with the mouth;
third, committing grave evil deeds with the mind.
Fourth, giving rise to the view of annihilationism;
fifth, giving rise to the view of eternalism;
sixth, giving rise to the view of causelessness.
Seventh, they give rise to the view of non-action;
eighth, they give rise to the view of nihilism;
ninth, they give rise to the view of extremes.
Tenth, failing to acknowledge or repay kindness.
By these ten karmas, one receives retribution in the hells.
Furthermore, there are ten karmas that cause sentient beings to receive the retribution of animals:
First, committing middling evil karma through bodily actions;
second, committing middling evil karma through verbal actions;
third, committing middling evil karma through mental actions.
Fourth, from the affliction of greed, various evil karmas arise;
fifth, from the affliction of hatred, various evil karmas arise;
sixth, from the affliction of delusion, various evil karmas arise.
Seventh, reviling sentient beings;
eighth, harassing and harming sentient beings;
ninth, giving impure things as gifts.
Tenth, engaging in sexual misconduct.
By these ten karmas, one receives the retribution of an animal.
Furthermore, there are ten karmas that cause sentient beings to receive the retribution of a hungry ghost:
First, performing minor evil deeds with the body;
second, performing minor evil deeds with speech;
third, performing minor evil deeds with the mind.
Fourth, the arising of excessive greed;
fifth, the arising of evil greed; sixth, jealousy; and—
Seventh, holding wrong views;
eighth, dying while being attached to the necessities of life;
ninth, perishing due to hunger.
Tenth, they die of parching thirst.
By these ten karmas, one receives the retribution of a hungry ghost (preta).
Furthermore, there are ten karmas that can cause sentient beings to receive the retribution of an asura:
First, performing subtle unwholesome deeds with the body;
second, performing subtle unwholesome deeds with the mouth;
third, performing subtle unwholesome deeds with the mind.
Fourth is arrogance; fifth is the conceit of "I am";
sixth is overweening pride.
Seventh, great pride; eighth, false pride;
ninth, pride of pride.
Tenth, one dedicates all roots of goodness toward rebirth in the asura realm.
By means of these ten karmas, one receives the retribution of an asura.
Furthermore, there are ten karmas that enable sentient beings to receive the retribution of the human realm:
First, not killing; second, not stealing;
third, not engaging in sexual misconduct.
Fourth, refraining from false speech;
fifth, refraining from frivolous speech;
sixth, refraining from divisive speech;
Seventh, not using harsh speech;
eighth, not being covetous;
ninth, not being angry.
Tenth, one does not hold wrong views.
By practicing these ten wholesome courses of action with some deficiency or incompleteness, one receives the retribution of the human realm.

Furthermore, there are ten types of karma that enable sentient beings to obtain the retribution of the desire-realm heavens, namely, the complete cultivation of the superior ten wholesome courses of action.

“Furthermore, there are ten karmas that enable sentient beings to obtain rebirth in the form heavens (*rūpa-deva*), namely: practicing the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśala*) with outflows (*sāsrava*) in conjunction with meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, there are four karmas that enable sentient beings to obtain rebirth in the formless heavens (*ārūpya-deva*):

first, transcending all perceptions of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), extinguishing perceptions of sensory resistance (*pratigha-saṃjñā*), and so forth, one enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samāpatti*).”
Second, transcending the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space, one enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness;
third, transcending the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness;
fourth, transcending the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness, one enters the meditative absorption of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
By means of these four karmas, one obtains rebirth as a formless deity (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Furthermore, there is karma that can cause sentient beings to obtain a definite retribution:

if a person, with a resolute mind, makes offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, or those who uphold the precepts, and dedicates this wholesome karma through the making of vows, they will immediately attain rebirth there.
This is called karma of determinate retribution.
Furthermore, there is karma that causes sentient beings to obtain indeterminate retribution:

if an action is not performed with an intensified mind, is not further cultivated, and is neither accompanied by the making of vows nor the dedication of merit for rebirth, this is called karma of indeterminate retribution.
Furthermore, there is karma that causes sentient beings to receive retribution as inhabitants of borderlands:

if one does not offer gifts with a resolute mind before the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, those who purely uphold the precepts, or the great assembly, yet dedicates this root of goodness with the aspiration to be born in a borderland.
By virtue of such a vow, one is born in a borderland and receives both pure and impure retributions.
Furthermore, there is karma that can cause sentient beings to receive retribution in a central land:

if, at the time of performing an action, one gives with exceptional and profound reverence toward the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, those who purely maintain the precepts, practitioners of the holy life, and the great assembly.

By means of these roots of goodness, they resolutely make a vow to seek rebirth in a central land, where they may again encounter a Buddha, hear the true Dharma, and receive the supreme, wondrous, and pure karmic rewards.
Furthermore, there is karma that causes sentient beings to exhaust their lifespan in hell:

if there are sentient beings who, having already committed karmic acts leading to hell, lack shame and dread of blame, feel no revulsion toward them, harbor no fear in their hearts, and instead give rise to joy; moreover, they do not repent, but further create and increase heavy evil karma, such as Devadatta and others.
Because of these karmic actions, they exhaust the full lifespan of the hells.
Furthermore, there are karmic actions that cause sentient beings to fall into hell and die prematurely before their lifespan is exhausted:

if a sentient being has accumulated karmic actions leading to hell, but subsequently gives rise to fear, shame, and revulsion, and repents and abandons them with a lack of resolute resolve (*anadhimukti*).
Due to such karma, one falls into hell;
however, because of subsequent remorse, one’s life in hell is cut short by half, and one does not exhaust its full lifespan.
Furthermore, there is karma that causes sentient beings to fall into hell, yet they enter it only briefly before emerging:

If there are sentient beings who have committed karmic deeds leading to hell, and having done so, they feel fear, give rise to superior faith, develop a sense of shame and remorse, loathe and abandon such actions, and perform earnest repentance—never again committing such grave offenses as King Ajātaśatru’s patricide—they may briefly enter hell but will immediately attain liberation.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If a person commits a grave offense, And having done so, deeply reproaches themselves,
Repenting and vowing not to do it again, They can uproot the karma of their fundamental nature."
"Furthermore, there is karma that is performed but not accumulated:

if there are sentient beings who commit various evil deeds through body, speech, and mind, yet having committed them, they feel fear, shame, and remorse, distancing themselves from such acts, deeply repenting and reproaching themselves, and never committing them again—this is called performing but not accumulating."
"Furthermore, there is karma that is accumulated but not performed:
if there are sentient beings who do not perform an action themselves, yet because of an evil mind, they incite others to commit evil, this is called 'accumulated but not performed.'
"Furthermore, there is karma that is both performed and accumulated:

if sentient beings, having committed various karmas, do not feel remorse or change their minds, but instead commit them repeatedly and also exhort others to do so, this is called both performing and accumulating."
"Furthermore, there is karma that is neither performed nor accumulated:
if a sentient being does not personally create karma, nor instructs others to do so—such as neutral (*avyākṛta*) karma and the like—this is called 'neither performed nor accumulated.'"
Furthermore, there is karma that is pleasant at first but bitter in the end:
if there are sentient beings who, being exhorted by others, joyfully practice giving, yet their resolve to give is not firm and they later feel regret.
By these causes and conditions, one is born among humans; though initially wealthy and joyful, one later returns to poverty and suffering.
This is called "suffering after initial happiness.
Furthermore, there is karma that is "suffering at first and happy afterward":

If there are sentient beings who, being exhorted by others, offer a small gift with some reluctance, yet feel joy upon giving and have no stinginess or regret in their hearts, they will, by these causes and conditions, be born among humans;
though poor and suffering at first, they will later become wealthy and happy.
This is called "suffering at first and happiness later.
Furthermore, there is karma that is suffering both at first and later:
if there are sentient beings who are separated from virtuous friends, who have no one to exhort and guide them, and are thus unable to practice even a small amount of giving.

By these causes and conditions, one is born into the human realm; being poor and suffering at the beginning, one remains poor and suffering at the end—this is called "suffering at the beginning and suffering at the end.
Furthermore, there is karma that is pleasant at the beginning and pleasant at the end:

if there are sentient beings who associate with virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra), who are exhorted to practice giving, and consequently give rise to joy and steadfastly cultivate the practice of generosity.
By these causes and conditions, one is born among humans, being wealthy and happy at the beginning and likewise wealthy and happy at the end.
Furthermore, there is karma for those who are poor yet delight in giving:
if there are sentient beings who previously practiced giving but did not encounter a field of merit, they transmigrate through birth and death and are reborn in the human realm.
Because they did not encounter fields of merit, their karmic rewards were meager and inferior, being exhausted as soon as they were obtained;
yet because they practiced giving, even while living in poverty, they were still able to practice generosity.
Furthermore, there are those whose karma is wealthy yet who remain stingy and greedy:
if there are sentient beings who have never practiced giving, yet encounter a virtuous friend and perform a single act of charity, meeting with a field of merit that is excellent.
Because the field is superior, their means of subsistence are abundant; yet because they have not practiced such deeds in the past, they remain stingy despite their wealth.
Furthermore, there is karma by which one is wealthy and able to give:
if sentient beings encounter spiritual friends, cultivate the practice of giving extensively, and meet with excellent fields of merit.
For these reasons, one may become immensely wealthy and possess abundant riches, yet still be able to practice generosity.
Furthermore, there is karma that leads to poverty and stinginess:
if sentient beings are separated from virtuous friends and have no one to exhort them, they are unable to practice generosity.
Due to these causes and conditions, one is born into poverty and remains stingy and greedy.
Furthermore, there is karma that can cause sentient beings to experience physical pleasure while their minds are not at ease, such as ordinary worldlings who possess merit.
"Furthermore, there is karma that can cause sentient beings to attain mental happiness while their bodies are not happy, such as an Arhat who lacks merit.
Furthermore, there is karma that can cause sentient beings to attain both physical and mental happiness, such as an Arhat who possesses merit."
“Furthermore, there is karma that causes sentient beings to experience neither pleasure in body nor pleasure in mind, such as that of an ordinary person lacking merit.
Furthermore, there is karma that causes the life-span of sentient beings to end while the karma does not end:

if there are sentient beings who die from hell and are reborn again in hell, or likewise among animals, hungry ghosts, humans, devas, asuras, and so forth—this is called the ending of life while the karma does not end.”
Furthermore, there are karmas that cause sentient beings' karma to be exhausted while their lifespan is not exhausted:

if there are sentient beings who, when pleasure is exhausted, experience suffering, or when suffering is exhausted, experience pleasure, and so forth, this is called the exhaustion of karma while the lifespan is not exhausted.
Furthermore, there is karma that causes both the karma and the life-span of sentient beings to be exhausted simultaneously:

if sentient beings pass away from the hells and are reborn among animals, hungry ghosts, or even humans, devas, asuras, and so forth, this is called the simultaneous exhaustion of both karma and life-span.
Furthermore, there is karma that causes both the karma and the life-span of sentient beings to be exhausted simultaneously:

if there are sentient beings who have exhausted all afflictions—namely, those such as the *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*—this is called the simultaneous exhaustion of both karma and life-span.

Furthermore, there is karma that causes sentient beings, even though they are born in the evil realms, to have exquisite physical forms, dignified eyes, and radiant complexions, such that people delight in beholding them:

if there are sentient beings who, due to the affliction of desire, give rise to the karma of breaking the precepts, by reason of these causes and conditions, although they are born in the evil realms, their forms are exquisite, their eyes are dignified, and their bodies are radiant, such that people delight in beholding them.
Furthermore, there is karma that causes sentient beings to be born in the evil realms with hideous appearances and coarse, rough skin and bodies, such that people do not delight in seeing them:

if there are sentient beings who, arising from the affliction of hatred, commit the karma of breaking the precepts, by reason of these causes and conditions, they are born in the evil realms with hideous appearances and coarse, rough skin and bodies, such that people do not delight in seeing them.
Furthermore, there is karma that causes sentient beings to be born in the evil realms with foul-smelling bodies and mouths, and impaired faculties.

If there are sentient beings who, arising from the affliction of delusion, commit the karma of breaking the precepts, by reason of these causes and conditions, they are born in the evil realms with foul-smelling bodies and mouths, and impaired faculties.
"Furthermore, there are ten karmas that result in external retribution of evil:
if sentient beings extensively cultivate the ten unwholesome karmas, they will cause all external objects to be incomplete."
First, due to the karma of killing, external retributions cause the great earth to become saline and barren, and medicinal herbs to lose their potency;
second, due to the karma of stealing, one brings about external frost, hail, locusts, and insects, causing famine in the world;
third, due to the karma of sexual misconduct, one brings about evil winds and rains, as well as various dust and grime.
Fourth, due to the karma of false speech, one brings about external objects that are entirely foul and putrid;
fifth, due to the karma of divisive speech, one brings about external lands that are uneven with high and low ground, steep cliffs, treacherous valleys, stumps, and brambles;

sixth, due to the karma of harsh speech, one brings about external retributions consisting of tiles, stones, sand, and gravel—coarse, rough, and unpleasant things that cannot be touched or approached.
Seventh, due to the karma of frivolous speech, an external retribution is experienced, causing the growth of dense forests of grasses and trees with branches and thorns;
eighth, due to the karma of greed, an external retribution is experienced, causing all crops and seeds to be minute and insignificant;
ninth, due to the karma of anger, an external retribution is experienced, causing the fruits of all trees to be bitter and astringent.
Tenth, due to the karma of wrong views, one receives external retribution: the crops are not substantial and the harvest is meager.
By means of these ten karmas, one obtains external evil retribution.
"Furthermore, there are ten karmas that result in external superior retribution:

if sentient beings cultivate the ten wholesome karmas, which are the opposite of the aforementioned [unwholesome] ones, it should be known that they will immediately obtain these ten external superior retributions."
"If there are sentient beings who prostrate before the stupas and temples of the Buddha, they shall obtain ten kinds of merit:
first, they shall obtain exquisite physical form and a beautiful voice;
second, whatever words they speak, all people will believe and submit to them."
Third, being fearless when among the multitude;
fourth, being cherished and protected by devas and humans;
fifth, being fully endowed with majestic power.
Sixth, all beings will come to him out of awe and submit themselves to him;
seventh, he will always be able to draw near to and attend upon the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
eighth, he will possess great merit and retribution.
Ninth, at the end of life, one is reborn in the heavens;
tenth, one swiftly realizes nirvana.
These are called the ten kinds of merit gained from paying homage to the stupas and temples of the Buddha.
"If there are sentient beings who offer precious canopies as gifts, they shall obtain ten kinds of merit:
first, they will dwell in the world like a canopy, providing shelter and protection for all sentient beings;
second, their bodies and minds will be peaceful and secure, free from all feverish afflictions."
Third, they will be respected by all, with no one daring to treat them with contempt;
fourth, they will possess great majesty and power;
fifth, they will always be able to draw near to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of great virtue and authority, taking them as their retinue.
Sixth, they constantly become wheel-turning sage-kings;
seventh, they always act as leaders in cultivating wholesome deeds;
eighth, they possess great merit and retribution.
Ninth, at the end of life, one is reborn in the heavens;
tenth, one swiftly realizes nirvana.
These are called the ten kinds of merit obtained from offering a precious canopy.
"If there are sentient beings who offer silk banners, they shall obtain ten kinds of merit:
first, they will stand like a banner in the world, being revered and supported by kings, ministers, relatives, and friends;
second, they will possess great wealth and resources, enjoying sovereign abundance."
Third, one's good reputation shall spread far and wide, reaching all directions;
fourth, one's physical appearance shall be dignified and handsome, and one's lifespan shall be long;
fifth, one shall always practice with firm resolve in whatever place of birth one is born.
Sixth, they possess great renown;
seventh, they possess great majesty and virtue;
eighth, they are born into noble lineages.
Ninth, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, one is reborn in the heavens;
tenth, one swiftly realizes nirvana.
These are called the ten kinds of merit obtained from the offering of silk banners.
"If there are sentient beings who offer bells and chimes, they shall obtain ten kinds of merit:
first, they shall obtain a Brahma-like voice;
second, they shall have great renown;"
Third, they naturally remember their past lives;
fourth, all who hear their words receive them with reverence;
fifth, they are always adorned with precious canopies.
Sixth, they possess exquisite necklaces as their adornment;
seventh, their countenances are upright and dignified, bringing joy to all who behold them;
eighth, they are endowed with great merit and retribution.
Ninth, at the end of life, one will be reborn in the heavens;
tenth, one will swiftly realize nirvana.
These are called the ten kinds of merit obtained from the offering of bells and chimes.
"If there are sentient beings who respectfully offer clothing, they shall obtain ten kinds of merit:
first, their faces and eyes will be dignified and handsome;
second, their skin will be fine and smooth."
Third, they are not defiled by dust or grime;
fourth, at birth they are endowed with exquisite and superior garments;
fifth, their bodies are covered with subtle and wonderful bedding.
Sixth, being clothed in the raiment of shame and modesty;
seventh, being loved and respected by all who see them;
eighth, possessing great wealth and treasures.
Ninth, at the end of life, one is reborn in the heavens;
tenth, one swiftly realizes nirvana.
These are called the ten kinds of merit obtained from the offering of clothing.
"If there are sentient beings who respectfully offer vessels, they shall obtain ten kinds of merit:
first, dwelling in the world like a vessel;
second, obtaining the moistening grace of wholesome dharmas."
Third, they are free from all thirst and craving;
fourth, whenever they thirst and think of water, flowing springs gush forth;
fifth, they shall never be born among the hungry ghosts.
Sixth, one obtains a sublime celestial vessel;
seventh, one remains far removed from evil associates;
eighth, one is endowed with great merit and retribution.
Ninth, one will be reborn in the heavens after the end of life;
tenth, one will swiftly realize nirvana.
These are called the ten kinds of merit obtained from making offerings of utensils.
"If there are sentient beings who offer food and drink, they shall obtain ten kinds of merit:
first, they obtain life;
second, they obtain physical beauty;"
Third, attaining power;
fourth, obtaining peaceful and unimpeded eloquence;
fifth, attaining fearlessness.
Sixth, being free from all indolence, one will be revered by the multitude;
seventh, one will be loved and cherished by all people;
eighth, one will possess great merit and retribution.
Ninth, at the end of life, one is reborn in the heavens;
tenth, one swiftly realizes nirvana.
These are called the ten kinds of merit obtained from offering food and drink.
"If there are sentient beings who offer boots and shoes, they shall obtain ten kinds of merit:
first, they will be endowed with a sublime vehicle;
second, the soles of their feet will be level and firm."
Third, the insteps of the feet are soft and supple;
fourth, they are light and agile when traveling long distances;
fifth, the body never experiences exhaustion.
Sixth, wherever they travel, their feet will not be injured by thorns, brambles, or rubble;
seventh, they will attain the power of supernatural faculties;
eighth, they will be provided with all necessary attendants.
Ninth, one will be reborn in the heavens at the end of life;
tenth, one will swiftly realize nirvana.
These are called the ten kinds of merit obtained from the offering of shoes.
"If there are sentient beings who offer incense and flowers, they shall obtain ten kinds of merit:
first, they will dwell in the world like a flower;
second, their bodies will be free from foul odors."
Third, the fragrance of merit and the fragrance of precepts pervade all directions;
fourth, wherever one is born, the faculty of the nose remains unimpaired;
fifth, one excels the world and becomes an object of refuge and veneration for the multitude.
Sixth, the body is always fragrant and pure;
seventh, one loves and delights in the True Dharma, receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting it;
eighth, one possesses great merit and retribution.
Ninth, at the end of life, one is reborn in the heavens;
tenth, one swiftly realizes nirvana.
These are called the ten kinds of merit obtained from offering incense and flowers.
"If there are sentient beings who offer lamps as a gift, they shall obtain ten kinds of merit:
first, they shall illuminate the world like a lamp;
second, in whatever place they are born, their physical eyes shall not be impaired."
Third, one attains the divine eye;
fourth, regarding wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, one attains excellent wisdom;
fifth, one eliminates and extinguishes the great darkness.
Sixth, one attains the clarity of wisdom;
seventh, while transmigrating through the world, one never remains in places of darkness;
eighth, one is endowed with great merit and retribution.
Ninth, at the end of life, one is reborn in the heavens;
tenth, one swiftly realizes nirvana.
These are called the ten kinds of merit obtained by offering lamps.
"If there are sentient beings who pay respect with palms joined, they shall obtain ten kinds of merit:
first, they shall obtain superior karmic rewards;
second, they shall be born into a noble family;"
Third, one obtains a supreme and wondrous form;
fourth, one obtains a supreme and wondrous voice;
fifth, one obtains a supreme and wondrous parasol.
Sixth, one attains supreme and wondrous eloquence;
seventh, one attains supreme and wondrous faith;
eighth, one attains supreme and wondrous precepts.
Ninth, one attains superior and wondrous extensive learning;
tenth, one attains superior and wondrous wisdom.
These are called the ten kinds of merit obtained through reverently joining the palms.
When the World-Honored One had finished preaching this Dharma, the elder Śuka conceived pure faith in the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, Śuka prostrated himself before the Buddha and spoke these words:
"I now invite the Buddha to go to the city of Śrāvastī, to the home of my father, the elder Traita."
"May my father and all sentient beings enjoy peace and happiness for a long night!
At that time, for the sake of benefiting them, the World-Honored One silently accepted the invitation.
Hearing what the Buddha had said, Śuka was filled with great joy; he prostrated himself and withdrew.
The Sūtra on the Differences in Karmic Retribution Spoken by the Buddha for the Elder Śuka.
